## Abstract

Multiple myeloma is a bone marrow (BM) plasma cell malignancy preceded by precursor conditions. BM biopsies are conducted infrequently and can yield inconclusive results due to technical limitations. Profiling circulating tumor cells (CTCs) may enable non-invasive routine clinical assessments but remains challenging. To address this, we describe a single-cell sequencing workflow to interrogate few tumor cells (SWIFT-seq), and employ single-cell RNA- and B cell receptor (BCR)-seq on paired BM and CTCs from 101 patients and healthy donors. We establish a sequencing-based CTC enumeration strategy and develop a CTC classifier to infer cytogenetic abnormalities. Additionally, we leverage expression profiling to measure tumor’s proliferative index in CTCs, and demonstrate clonal dynamics can be captured in CTCs. Lastly, we propose a model whereby tumor burden, proliferation, cytogenetics and a circulatory capacity signature influence CTC burden. Overall, SWIFT-seq may advance blood-based myeloma diagnostics, surveillance, and prognostication, and reveal biological mechanisms of tumor dissemination.

## Introduction

Multiple myeloma (MM), a plasma cell malignancy of the bone marrow (BM), is consistently preceded by two precursor conditions: an initial state, called monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), followed by smoldering multiple myeloma (SMM)1–4. BM biopsies remain the gold standard for staging and restaging patients across the disease spectrum, however, they are invasive and painful procedures that are seldom used for continuous monitoring, especially in the precursor disease setting1,2,5. Additionally, MM is a spatially heterogeneous disease, where a single-site BM biopsy may not provide comprehensive information on tumor burden and disease biology occurring throughout the body6–8.

Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are detectable in the peripheral blood (PB) of patients with MM and precursor disease using multiparametric flow cytometry (MFC) or next-generation flow (NGF, EuroFlow) cytometry and the CellSearch platform9–14. CTC quantification has shown prognostic value as CTC levels positively correlate with disease stage and risk status in precursor and active MM patients and can be used to monitor treatment response and predict disease relapse9–25. Most recently, CTC levels were reported to outperform BM infiltration estimates for progression risk assessment in patients with SMM, challenging current clinical paradigms that rely on BM biopsies for risk stratification26. Genomic profiling has demonstrated that CTCs harbor the same copy number abnormalities, translocations and mutations as BM tumor cells, and that serial CTC profiling can help track clonal dynamics to detect the emergence of high-risk subclones in PB11,27–29. Transcriptomic profiling has also shown concordant gene expression profiles between CTCs and BM tumor cells, and CTC-specific genes that associate with prognosis and suggest hypoxia-induced mechanisms that may promote CTC egression from the BM27,30,31. Nevertheless, CTC profiling is still not widely performed for clinical assessments and most published studies supporting the clinical utility of CTCs have significant limitations, including (1) focusing on CTC enumeration alone, (2) profiling small cohorts predominantly of patients with advanced disease, and (3) use of bulk sequencing which may be confounded by normal plasma cell and immune cell contamination. Additional studies are warranted that can sensitively differentiate malignant and normal plasma cells in the PB from patients representing the entire disease continuum to understand the biological features that influence tumor cell circulation dynamics and explore the clinical utility of CTCs past enumeration.

In this study, we describe a single-cell sequencing workflow to interrogate few tumor cells (SWIFT-seq), that enables comprehensive analyses of CTCs using a single approach32. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell B cell receptor sequencing (scBCR-seq) on paired CD138-positive (CD138+) BM tumor cell and CTC samples from 73 patients with MGUS, SMM, and newly diagnosed MM (NDMM) and 28 healthy donors. First, we establish a sequencing-based enumeration strategy that can successfully quantify CTCs without normal plasma cell contamination and demonstrate a progressive increase in CTCs with advanced disease, validating this approach. Next, we demonstrate further clinical utility by using scRNA-seq to reliably infer translocations and copy number abnormalities, providing an alternative strategy to cytogenetic clinical testing using BM biopsies. Subsequently, we utilize the tandem molecular profiling to interrogate both the proliferation index and the circulatory capacity of tumor cells which hold prognostic value. Lastly, we demonstrate scRNA-seq of CTCs can successfully capture the clonal dynamics observed in BM tumor cells. Notably, using SWIFT-seq, we also shed light on features that drive the egress of malignant cells from the BM into the PB and propose a four-pronged model, whereby tumor burden, cycling, cytogenetics, and circulatory capacity all contribute to shaping CTC burden. Overall, we demonstrated the validity of single-cell profiling of CTCs to provide biological insights as well as layers of clinical information using a single method, which was successful even in the most technically challenging setting of patients with precursor disease and few CTCs.

## Results

### ScRNA-seq coupled with scBCR-seq efficiently enumerates CTCs

To evaluate the capacity of droplet-based single-cell sequencing to profile CTCs from patients with precursor and active MM, we performed coupled single-cell RNA/BCR-seq on CD138+ plasma cells from 201 samples, including paired BM and PB samples from 73 patients (MGUS: n=14; SMM, n=41; NDMM, n=18), and 28 healthy donors (Fig. 1a; Supplementary Table 1). Malignant plasma cells were identified based on their V(D)J sequences, instead of relying on aberrantly expressed markers that are not universally expressed across tumors (Extended Fig. 1a, b; Supplementary Table 2)33–36. After filtering, we obtained a total of 1,292,479 CD138+ plasma cells for subsequent analyses, including 741,389 malignant and 327,047 normal plasma cells from BM and 87,823 CTCs and 136,220 normal plasma cells from PB (Fig. 1b).

As expected, normal plasma cells grouped together, while malignant cells from patients clustered separately in a patient-specific manner, reflecting the unique transcriptional profile of each tumor (Extended Fig. 1c). Malignant and normal plasma cells separated by compartments, with CTCs clustering closest to their matched BM tumor cells, indicating transcriptional similarity but not complete uniformity (Fig. 1b; Extended Fig. 1b,c). CTCs were detected in 90% (n=66/73; 95% CI: 81-96%) of patients in the cohort (MGUS: 71%, SMM: 95%, NDMM: 94%) and 88% (n=58/66; 95% CI: 77-94%) of patients with detectable CTCs had at least 10 CTCs. The number of CTCs analyzed per sample ranged from 1 to 27,388, with a median of 204 CTCs per patient (Fig. 1c; Supplementary Table 3). To account for differences in the number of plasma cells captured per sample, we opted for using the proportion of malignant plasma cells out of all plasma cells in the PB for sequencing-based enumeration. To assess the clinical relevance of this metric, we compared this proportion across disease stages. The proportion of malignant plasma cells out of all plasma cells in the PB increased significantly with disease progression from MGUS (median: ~1%) to SMM (~16%), and NDMM (~66%) (two-sided Wilcoxon, MGUS vs SMM: q=0.022; SMM vs NDMM: q=0.022; MGUS vs NDMM: q=0.0074) (Fig. 1d). These results suggest that sequencing-based CTC enumeration captures prognostically relevant differences in tumor burden, with the added benefit of providing transcriptomic profiling in tandem. There was a positive correlation between BM infiltration and CTC burden (two-sided Pearson’s, r=0.56, p=3.4e-07) (Extended Fig. 1d), however, CTC levels were variable even within groups of patients with similar tumor burden and clinical staging (Fig. 1e).

### SWIFT-seq reliably infers cytogenetic abnormalities

Cytogenetic profiling by Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH) is used as standard of care for risk stratification in patients with SMM/MM5,37. However, FISH requires a BM biopsy and its sensitivity can be limited by the number of myeloma cells detected, particularly for patients with low tumor burden. In our cohort, FISH was performed on cells obtained from the first BM aspirate pull, following plasma cell enrichment. Nevertheless, 64% (95% CI: 36-86) of patients with MGUS, 51% (95% CI: 35-67) of patients with SMM, and 28% (95% CI: 11-54) of patients with NDMM were unclassified by FISH (Extended Fig. 2a; Supplementary Table 1). To expand the clinical utility of scRNA-seq of CTCs beyond enumeration, we explored the feasibility of using small numbers of CTCs to infer primary cytogenetic abnormalities, such as hyperdiploidy (HRD) and IgH translocations.

To systematically classify cytogenetic events in patients, we trained a multinomial logistic regression model on 50 primary BM tumors from patients that were successfully cytogenetically classified either by FISH (n=38) or research-level whole-genome sequencing (WGS) when available (n=36). An additional single patient with t(8;14) (IgH-MAFA) translocation detected via WGS was not considered for training to avoid overfitting. Key translocation partner genes were upregulated in accordance with translocation type identified by FISH or WGS in both BM tumor cells and CTCs (Fig. 2a). The model leverages key translocation partner genes and well-established RNA signatures that correspond to underlying cytogenetic profiles and uses HRD as reference (Fig. 2b)38. We performed leave-one-out cross-validation and aggregated results from the 50 held-out samples. We observed remarkable performance with 49 out of 50 cases correctly classified (98%; 95% CI: 88-100) (Fig. 2c). The one case with t(4;14) that was misclassified as “No Trx” (i.e., no IgH translocation) was an outlier case with 15 CTCs, no FGFR3 expression and the lowest NSD2 expression out of all cases with t(4;14). Next, we aggregated coefficients from the 50 leave-one-out models by taking the median and generated an aggregate model. Applying this BM-trained model on matched CTC samples from the training cohort (n=46; four tumors from the training cohort did not have CTCs), where we observed high accuracy (n=46/46 or 100%; 95% CI: 90-100) (Fig. 2d).

To obtain the final classification of tumors in our cohort, we applied the aggregate model on all tumors (separately for the BM and the PB). Tumors without an IgH translocation were classified as HRD when copy number variant inference via Numbat detected at least two extra chromosomal copies39; otherwise, they were classified as “Other” (n=7). Four out of seven “Other” tumors had CNVs detected but did not meet HRD criteria; the remaining three had no CNVs detected. As no patients with t(8;14) or t(6;14) were included in the training cohort, we manually classified one patient with t(8;14) by WGS and with high MAFA/ITGB7 expression as MAFA Trx and two patients with high CCND3 expression as CCND3 Trx. Additionally, two patients were classified as MAF Trx only in their CTCs, but showed consistently high expression of MAF, ITGB7, and the MF signature in both their CTCs and their BM, and thus were classified as MAF Trx. Lastly, one patient was classified as NSD2 Trx in their CTCs only, but the overall expression of NSD2, FGFR3, and the MS signature was low, so in the absence of HRD, they were classified as “Other”. Overall, we classified the majority of cases that had previously unknown primary cytogenetic abnormalities (Fig. 2e), unlocking CTC-based cytogenetic classification that can enable testing during routine blood draws and may improve prognostication and therapy selection.

IgH translocations and HRD are primary oncogenic events, and once detected, regular testing is only executed for the detection of high-risk secondary genomic abnormalities that may be acquired over time. Thus, we examined the reliability of capturing copy number abnormalities using scRNA-seq and demonstrated it recapitulates results obtained from BM FISH clinical testing; 4/4 patients displayed Del17p (sensitivity of 100%; 95% CI: 40-100), 5/6 patients displayed Del13q (sensitivity of 83%; 95% CI: 37-99), and 13/15 patients displayed Amp1q (sensitivity of 87%; 95% CI: 58-98). Moreover, scRNA-seq was able to identify additional high-risk abnormalities, which were either not identified by FISH (Amp1q, n=3; Del13q, n=2) or not tested by FISH (Del13q, n=21), (Fig. 2f, Extended Fig. 2b). Therefore, scRNA-seq could reliably detect both IgH translocations/HRD and high-risk secondary genomic abnormalities. This is despite the fact that early aspirate pulls are used for clinical-grade FISH testing while subsequent pulls, which typically contain fewer tumor cells, are used for research-level assays like scRNA-seq40,41.

Next, we set out to determine the lowest number of CTCs needed for successful inference of primary cytogenetic abnormalities. We randomly downsampled a range of tumor cells (1-100) from each CTC sample with 10 iterations per cell number and used our aggregate model to classify samples. We observed a strong overall performance with as few as 10 CTCs, and a deterioration of performance below that threshold (Fig. 2g). Overall, we concluded 10 CTCs were enough for at least 90% of cases to be classified correctly in at least 90% of the iterations (Fig. 2h). This is important since 79.5% of patients in our cohort had at least 10 CTCs detected, including 87% (n=13/15) of patients with high-risk SMM (HRSMM) (95% CI: 58-98) and 94% (n=17/18) of patients with NDMM (95% CI: 71-100) (Fig. 1c). Therefore, this approach can correctly classify patients that may receive treatment and benefit the most from cytogenetic profiling for patient outcome prediction and management.

Finally, we leveraged our improved cytogenetic classification to explore how cytogenetic abnormalities associate with CTC burden. Compared to patients with HRD tumors, patients with NSD2 and MAF translocations had significantly higher CTC levels in their PB (two-sided Wilcoxon, q=0.014 and q=0.012, respectively) (Figure 2i). Importantly, in a multivariate linear model, both disease stage (NDMM vs MGUS, p=0.0022) and cytogenetics were significant predictors of CTC burden, with NSD2 Trx (p=0.006), MAF Trx (p=8.15e-05), and MAFB Trx (p=0.044) significantly associated with CTC burden. We validated this observation in the CoMMpass cohort (n=625), where patients with t(4;14) and t(14;16) translocations had significantly higher CTC burden compared to patients with HRD tumors (two-sided Wilcoxon, q=0.0036 and q=3.3e-10, respectively) (Extended Figure 2c). Patients with t(11;14) in the CoMMpass cohort were also shown to have significantly higher CTC burden compared to patients with HRD tumors (q=0.00011). Lastly, in our cohort, patients with Amp1q and Del13q had significantly higher CTC burden (two-sided Wilcoxon, p=0.023 and p=0.043, respectively), which was also validated in the CoMMpass cohort (p=5.3e-05 and p=0.0011, respectively) (Figure 2j,k; Extended Figure 2d,e). These results support the hypothesis that cytogenetic abnormalities may influence the patient’s CTC burden, independent of disease stage and tumor burden.

### Tumor proliferative capacity is associated with CTC burden

Prior studies have shown that plasma cell proliferative index (PCPI) holds prognostic value in MM42–46. However, slide-based or flow cytometry-based tests to measure tumor proliferation index require a BM biopsy and have not been broadly adopted in clinical practice beyond few institutions. Previous studies have reported that CTCs from MM patients are mostly quiescent, however, this was assessed with technologies less sensitive than scRNA-seq13,47. We aimed to assess whether scRNA-seq can capture proliferative CTCs, which could enable the measurement of the tumor’s proliferative index from the PB when a BM biopsy may not be feasible. First, we compared the proportion of cycling cells in BM tumor cells and CTCs. To control for the lower probability of detecting cycling tumor cells in patients with too few tumor cells, we limited our analyses to tumors with at least 100 CTCs (n=43). Most tumor cells from both compartments were quiescent, and BM tumor cells had significantly more cells in S phase (0.69%, two-sided paired Wilcoxon, q=8e-04) and, less so, in G2M phase (0.25%, q=0.73) compared to CTCs (0.15% and 0.08%, respectively) (Fig. 3a, 3b). Interestingly, with single-cell resolution we could detect populations of cycling CTCs in 72% (n=31/43, 95% CI: 56-84) of tumors (Fig. 3b). Moreover, tumors with higher cycling capacity in the BM-resident tumor cells (> median) had significantly more cycling CTCs (two-sided Wilcoxon, p=0.0062) (Fig. 3c). Excluding outliers (n=4), the CTC proliferative index positively correlated with that of BM tumor cells, indicating that it may be a complementary strategy to assessing BM tumor cell proliferation (two-sided Pearson’s r=0.53, p=0.00055) (Extended Fig. 3). Overall, these results suggest that scRNA-seq of CTCs can capture the tumor’s proliferative index, in addition to enabling enumeration and cytogenetic classification.

Next, we explored whether tumor proliferative capacity may be associated with CTC burden. We separated patients into those with low and high BM tumor cycling capacity (> median), and observed significantly higher CTC burden in patients with higher tumor cycling capacity (two-sided Wilcoxon, p=0.00028) (Figure 3d), and validated this association in the CoMMpass cohort (two-sided Wilcoxon, p=9.8e-09) (Figure 3e). Since CTC burden and tumor cycling capacity are known to increase with disease progression, and we showed cytogenetics impacts CTC burden, we next fit a Gaussian model on CTC burden using disease stage, the proportion of cycling tumor cells, and cytogenetics as covariates. We observed that disease stage, tumor cycling, and the presence of NSD2 Trx, MAF Trx, and MAFB Trx are independently associated with CTC burden (Figure 3f). Overall, these results suggest a model whereby disease stage, tumor cytogenetics, and tumor cycling capacity independently shape CTC burden.

### Tumor circulatory capacity contributes to CTC burden

To understand how CTCs may differ from BM tumor cells transcriptionally, we systematically compared gene expression between paired CTCs and BM tumor cells across patients with at least 30 tumor cells in each compartment (n=51), and identified genes that were significantly upregulated (two-sided Wilcoxon, q < 0.05 & log fold-change > 0) in at least 60% of BM-CTC pairs (n=827) (Fig. 4a). Pathway enrichment analysis of hits revealed frequent upregulation of Myc signaling, PI3K-Akt signaling, interferon response, TNFα signaling via NF-κB, inflammation, hypoxia, and metabolic pathways (one-sided hypergeometric, q < 0.05) (Fig. 4b).

Next, we sorted genes by the number of CTC samples they were upregulated in, as well as their average log fold-change in those samples, and empirically derived a circulatory signature out of the top 100 genes. This circulatory signature contained genes that were significantly upregulated in at least 78% of CTC samples and did not overlap with established myeloma signatures related to tumor cytogenetics and/or prognosis (Figure 4c). We hypothesized that patients whose BM tumor cells show high circulatory scores may have higher CTC burden. To identify tumor cells with high circulatory capacity in the patient BM, we asked that their circulatory score be higher than the 1st quartile of the CTC distribution. We then computed the proportion of tumor cells with high circulatory capacity within each tumor and separated patients to those with high BM circulatory capacity (> median) and those with low. We observed that patients with higher BM circulatory capacity had significantly higher CTC burden (two-sided Wilcoxon, p=0.0018) (Figure 4d). To validate this observation, we scored patients in the CoMMpass cohort by taking the mean expression of signature genes per individual (n=99/100 present in the dataset) and split patients based on the median. Again, patients with high BM circulatory scores in the CoMMpass cohort had significantly higher CTC burden (two-sided Wilcoxon, p=2.5e-18) (Figure 4e). Additionally, in both our cohort and the CoMMpass cohort, patients with MAF Trx and MAFB Trx, who have high CTC burden, showed significantly higher BM circulatory scores compared to patients with HRD (Figure 4f,g). Notably, this is despite the minimal overlap in genes between cytogenetics-specific signatures and the circulatory capacity signature. Furthermore, in the CoMMpass cohort, patients with t(11;14) and t(4;14), who we previously showed have significantly higher CTC burden compared to HRD patients in the same cohort, also had significantly higher BM circulatory scores. Overall, these results suggest that the circulatory capacity signature may partially explain the impact of cytogenetics on CTC burden. In a multivariate linear model, high BM circulatory capacity, tumor cycling capacity and disease stage were all independent predictors of CTC burden (Figure 4h). Lastly, a high BM circulatory capacity score was associated with significantly shorter overall survival (OS) in the CoMMpass cohort (two-sided log-rank, p=6.4e-07) and this effect was independent of cytogenetics, with both high BM circulatory score and t(4;14) status maintaining their negative impact on OS (High BM Circulatory Score: p=5.29e-06; t(4;14): p=0.0289) (Figure 4i). Collectively, these results suggest a four-pronged model whereby disease stage, tumor cytogenetics, tumor cycling capacity and circulatory capacity all contribute to shaping CTC burden.

### CTCs capture the clonal dynamics of tumor cells in the BM

To investigate the degree to which CTC samples reflected the genomic complexity of tumor cells detected in the paired BM biopsy site, we utilized Numbat to identify subclonal copy number variants (CNVs) and constructed phylogenetic trees39. A total of 58 tumors had CNVs detected and in 56/58 of these tumors we identified subclones. We systematically compared the frequency of clones between BM/PB compartments across tumors with subclones and at least 100 CTCs (n=35). We observed a strong positive correlation between clone frequency in the BM and CTCs (two-sided Pearson’s, r=0.9, p=2.7e-44), suggesting that CTCs capture the genomic heterogeneity and clonal dynamics of tumor cells in the BM (Fig. 5a). Notably, in certain cases, clones carrying high-risk features were overrepresented in the PB. For example, in one patient (Patient #70), a subclone carrying Del13q (clone 3) had a frequency of 28.3% (95% CI: 26.3-30.3%) in the BM but a frequency of 63.6% (95% CI: 61.4-65.7%) in the PB (Fig. 5b–e). In another patient, (Patient #20), a subclone carrying Del17p (clone 5) had a frequency of 8.3% (95% CI: 7.1-9.6%) in the BM but a frequency of 21.5% (95% CI: 19.7-23.4%) in the PB (Fig. 5f–i). Overall, these results suggest that scRNA-seq of CTCs can be used to characterize the genomic landscape of tumor cells, and could enable more routine surveillance for the detection of high-risk abnormalities for patients with MM and its precursor conditions.

Lastly, to deconvolve the impact of secondary CNVs on CTC burden, we leveraged patients with subclonal Amp1q (n=12) and subclonal Del13q (n=20) and compared the circulatory capacity of BM tumor cells with the abnormalities to the rest of the respective tumors, which inherently accounts for the tumor’s cytogenetic background. This is important as cytogenetic classes that are associated with high CTC burden, such as t(4;14) and t(14;16), are known to frequently acquire high-risk secondary CNVs such as Amp1q and Del13q. Notably, the % of BM tumor cells with high circulatory capacity was significantly higher in subclones carrying Amp1q and Del13q, compared to the rest of the tumor cells in those respective tumors (two-sided paired Wilcoxon, p<0.01) (Figure 5j, k). These results suggest that the impact of Amp1q and Del13q on CTC burden may be independent of the tumor’s cytogenetic background, and as these abnormalities are typically acquired over time, they may contribute to the increased CTC burden observed with disease progression.

## Discussion

BM biopsies are the gold standard for staging and genetic characterization of patients with precursor MM and MM37. However, their invasiveness limits routine sampling for restaging during disease surveillance. CTCs from tumor niches across the body may provide an alternative for risk stratification and monitoring. A key limitation is the low number of CTCs in PB, particularly in patients with low tumor burden. Here we introduced SWIFT-seq, an experimental and analytical workflow that utilized scRNA-seq and scBCR-seq on paired BM and CTCs from patients representing the MM disease continuum to sensitively detect and profile few CTCs. SWIFT-seq enabled the collection of clinically useful information and shed light on poorly understood biological mechanisms of tumor cell dissemination.

CTCs are detectable in precursor patients indicating that malignant cells in the BM acquire the ability to egress at premalignant stages9–13,20,22,24,26. Enumeration of CTCs has shown prognostic value, as elevated levels are associated with earlier disease progression and/or worse OS9,11–13,22,26. Leveraging scBCR-seq, we used clonotypic data to identify malignant plasma cells. This was advantageous over traditional approaches, such as flow cytometry and CellSearch, that leverage the aberrant expression of markers which may not be universally expressed by all MM tumors. Overall, we detected CTCs in 71% of patients with MGUS, 95% of patients with SMM, and 94% of patients with NDMM, which compares favorably with other methods11,13. Furthermore, we showed that sequencing-based enumeration recapitulates prognostically relevant differences in tumor burden across disease stages. Of note, our study cohort was a predominately white patient population and additional analyses are needed in racially and ethnically diverse patient populations. In contrast to other methods that solely provide CTC enumeration information, scRNA-seq additionally provides transcriptomic profiling which can be utilized in many ways, including for cytogenetic characterization.

Cytogenetic characterization using FISH can inform patient management and therapy selection48–53. In the active disease setting, patients with high-risk events may receive different upfront and maintenance therapy compared to standard-risk patients, and patients with t(11;14) may receive venetoclax54–57. In the precursor disease setting, patients with high-risk events may be more closely monitored or enroll in early intervention clinical trials5,37,58,59. However, patients can remain cytogenetically unclassified due to hemodilution and low tumor purity affecting the sensitivity of FISH results, and secondary genetic changes may go undetected due to infrequent BM sampling. In our cohort, 64% of patients with MGUS, 51% of patients with SMM, and 28% of patients with NDMM had insufficient plasma cells for FISH testing or were not classified as having a primary IgH translocation or HRD. This is despite the fact that FISH was performed after plasma cell enrichment and on the first aspirate pull, as per standard practice, which is less likely to show hemodilution41. In our cohort, scRNA-seq detected tumor cells in most patients, which suggests it may be used for cytogenetic classification. It is known that primary cytogenetic abnormalities, such as IgH translocations and hyperdiploidy, lead to specific transcriptional changes which can be captured by bulk or scRNA-seq27,31,33,35. However, whether such changes could be leveraged for reliable inference of cytogenetic abnormalities on small numbers of tumor cells had not been previously assessed. We demonstrated the ability of scRNA-seq to detect the presence of primary cytogenetic abnormalities in BM or CTC samples with 98-100% accuracy compared to FISH or WGS. Importantly, we inferred the presence of primary cytogenetic abnormalities in patients where BM FISH clinical testing was inconclusive or where FISH did not test for the abnormality in question (for example, t(8;14)), reducing the frequency of unclassified patients in our cohort from 48% to less than 10%, which is more in line with the frequency of patients who do not have a common primary IgH translocations or HRD60,61. Remarkably, we showed that we could correctly classify at least 90% of patients with 10 CTCs. We detected 10 CTCs in 94% of patients with NDMM and 87% of patients with HRSMM, two groups of patients who are eligible for treatment or enrollment into clinical trials and may benefit the most from accurate cytogenetic profiling. Our approach could also reliably detect secondary high-risk genomic abnormalities, such as Amp1q, Del13q, and Del17p, compared to FISH, and occasionally detect events missed by FISH. Of note, the rate of patients with NDMM that were unclassified by FISH in our cohort is higher than previously reported in a cohort of NDMM patients (28% vs. 15.8%) although gold-standard FISH testing was performed and patients were selected purely based on sample availability62. An additional limitation is that our model was trained on IgH translocations alone, but rare variants involving IgK or IgL have been observed before and could be indistinguishable from IgH translocations at the RNA level as the downstream transcriptional alterations may be identical61. Lastly, although technically challenging, mutation detection may also be possible from scRNA-seq data for coding mutations that are expressed, which could unlock additional clinically useful information in the future63–65. Overall, scRNA-seq of CTCs showcased that CTC-based cytogenetic profiling holds great potential for risk stratification and minimally invasive longitudinal monitoring of patients with MM and its precursor conditions. This represents only one additional layer of prognostically relevant information that scRNA-seq of CTCs can provide with enumeration, which differentiates this workflow from methods that provide enumeration only.

Another layer of prognostically relevant information that can be captured by scRNA-seq is the tumor’s proliferative index, which has not been broadly adopted in clinical practice. Prior studies had shown that CTCs are largely quiescent, however, using scRNA-seq we were able to detect proliferative CTCs in 72% of patients and demonstrate a positive correlation between the CTC proliferative index and that measured in BM tumor cells13,44,47. Previous studies have shown that a higher plasma cell proliferation index (PCPI) in the BM is associated with a higher progression rate and earlier time to progression in SMM patients to active MM42. Additionally, proliferation-associated gene expression signatures, like the PR signature, have been shown to portend poor outcome in patients with NDMM, independent of the tumor’s cytogenetic background38,61. Similarly, studies in solid cancers have reported that the presence of cycling CTCs is associated with significantly shorter OS in patients with metastatic breast and prostate cancer66,67. Our results suggest proliferative capacity may be measurable in PB samples and highlight another utility for scRNA-seq of CTCs which may hold clinical value in addition to simple enumeration and cytogenetic profiling.

Previous DNA sequencing studies have shown concordant genomic events detected in CTCs compared to the BM; although certain subclonal mutations may only be detectable in CTCs and not the BM, potentially because CTCs represent subclones from multiple BM niches across the body11,28,29,68. While the detection of abnormalities is important, the ability to successfully trace clonal dynamics, namely the size of subclones within the tumor which can change over time reflecting selection and genomic evolution, is required for clinical-grade genomic surveillance69. Here, we leveraged subclonal CNVs and reconstructed phylogenetic trees to compare the frequency of clones between the BM and PB and investigate how well the CTC pool captures the genomic complexity and clonal dynamics of BM tumor cells. We found that CTCs mirror the clonal dynamics observed in the BM with a significant positive correlation in clone frequency between the two compartments. Additionally, we identified cases where a subclone carrying high-risk features, such as Del13q and Del17p, had higher frequency in the PB compared to the BM, which highlights how scRNA-seq of CTCs could complement BM-based assays.

By comparing CTC samples to their paired BM tumor cells, we derived a circulatory score that was variably expressed in BM tumor cells, where patients with higher BM circulatory capacity have higher CTC burden. We validated this association in the CoMMpass cohort and also demonstrated that a high BM circulatory capacity score was associated with significantly shorter OS. Overall, circulatory capacity may also partly explain the impact of cytogenetics on CTC burden and is an independent predictor of CTC burden together with disease stage and tumor cycling. Collectively, our results suggest a model whereby tumor burden, cycling capacity, cytogenetics, and circulatory capacity may determine the patient’s CTC burden.

Our study demonstrates that SWIFT-seq can overcome the challenge of high-throughput detection and recovery of rare CTCs, without necessitating sophisticated enrichment practices. We highlight that in addition to CTC enumeration, scRNA-seq enables improved genomic characterization, as well as molecular profiling to assess tumor proliferative index and measure prognostically relevant gene expression signatures. Currently, four separate assays that are not widely performed would be needed to obtain the same level of characterization (including NGF for enumeration, FISH for cytogenetics, PCPI/PCPro for proliferation, and microarrays or bulk RNA-seq for gene expression profiling). Furthermore, three of these assays currently necessitate a BM biopsy as input and CTC levels from many patients with MGUS, SMM or MM post-therapy are too low to yield successful results from separate assay workflows. Overall, we contend that SWIFT-seq could be pivotal for advancing routine blood-based tumor profiling for patients and shedding light on the biology of tumor cell dissemination (Figure 6).

## Methods

### Patient sample collection

Patients and healthy donors (excluding purchased samples) enrolled in PCROWD or PROMISE studies at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and provided written informed consent for research use-based collection of samples (Institutional Review Board #14-174/#18-370). Research was carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Paired BM and PB samples from a cohort of 73 patients, including 14 patients with MGUS, 41 patients with SMM, and 18 patients with newly diagnosed MM (NDMM), and 28 healthy donors (13 paired BM and PB, 15 BM only) were prospectively collected. SMM patients were stratified based on the “20-2-20” risk model developed by the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG), which separates patients based on BM plasma cell infiltration (>20%), M-protein in the serum (>2g/dL), and free light-chain ratio (>20)5; this rendered 16 patients with low-risk SMM (LRSMM), 10 with intermediate-risk (IRSMM) and 15 with high-risk SMM (HRSMM). BM aspirates from 28 healthy donors were either purchased (AllCells, n=9) or obtained from surgically removed femoral head specimens from individuals who underwent hip arthroplasty due to osteoarthritis (n=19). Participants were considered healthy based on negative screening of abnormal M-protein by Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Time-of-Flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry, and no past/current cancer diagnosis. The median age of healthy donors was 56 (range: 48-88) vs. 64 (range: 35-85) in patients (two-sided Wilcoxon, p=0.27). Participants’ sex was not considered in the design of this study and no sex-related analyses were conducted. Patients had routine cytogenetics and FISH performed on BM biopsies and serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) and serum free light chain (SFLC) assay performed on PB in clinical-grade pathology labs.

Clinical-grade FISH testing was performed on the first BM aspirate pull at Mayo Clinic. For primary cytogenetic abnormalities, a patient was positive when the abnormality was present in any clinical FISH tests performed; for secondary CNVs, only FISH tests at the sample’s timepoint were considered. For Del13q specifically, we considered results at the sample’s timepoint or within 1 year prior, since Mayo Clinic’s progression panel does not include a Del13q probe. A Del13q probe was tested in 14/71 patients with FISH and tumor cells detected by scRNA-seq. For downstream analyses, patients with focal and arm-level CNVs in chr1q, chr13q, and chr17p were considered positive for respective abnormalities. One patient with trisomy 1 was considered positive for Amp1q. The % infiltration on the BM biopsy was used for downstream analyses, except in 1 case of an unsuccessful biopsy and a successful aspirate, where the aspirate measurement was used. In two patients where the infiltration on the biopsy was reported to be <10%, we considered the infiltration to be 9%. For two patients with MGUS no BM infiltration estimates were available.

A total of 201 samples were processed for this study, including 187 baseline and 14 serial samples (from 10 patients). For 21 samples, multiple aliquots were sequenced (2 aliquots for 19 samples/3 aliquots for 2 samples) and cells were combined across aliquots. The total number of libraries was 224. Tumor cells from baseline and serial samples were combined to increase power for tumor cell annotation and cytogenetic classification. All other analyses were performed using baseline samples only.

### Patient sample processing

BM aspirates (5-20mLs) and PB (30mLs) were drawn into EDTA tubes and stored at 4°C until processing within 6hrs, as previously described70. PB mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated using a two-step protocol; 1) erythrocytes were aggregated and sedimented (Miltenyi, #130-115-169) and 2) non-PBMCs were magnetically labeled with biotin-conjugated monoclonal antibodies targeting granulocytes and erythrocytes (Miltenyi, #130-115-169). Magnetically labelled non-PBMCs were separated within a MACS column (Miltenyi, #130-021-101) of an autoMACS Pro (Miltenyi, Cat #130-092-545), while unlabeled and untouched PBMCs remained for subsequent enrichment. BM mononuclear cells were isolated from aspirates using density gradient centrifugation. Briefly, BM was filtered to remove clots and/or debris (Miltenyi, #130-098-463), diluted 1:3 with 1X Phosphate-Buffered Saline (PBS) (Corning, #MT21040CV), and poured above 15mLs of Ficoll-Paque medium (Cytvia, #45001750) within a SepMate™ PBMC isolation tube (StemCell, #85450), as previously described70. After centrifugation at 1,200 x g for 15 minutes, PBMCs were poured away from unwanted cells and washed twice with cold 1xPBS prior to plasma cell enrichment using CD138 magnetic beads, as previously described70. BM underwent single-column positive selection and PB a double-column positive selection due to the lower frequency of CTCs and desire for higher purity (Miltenyi, #130-097-614).

### Single-cell RNA/V(D)J library construction and sequencing

Sequencing libraries were prepared from fresh BMs and CTCs, including 5’ scRNA-seq and scBCR-seq libraries. Cells were centrifuged at 300 x g for 5 mins and washed with cold 0.1% Ultrapure Bovine Serum Albumin (BSA)/PBS buffer (Invitrogen, #AM2616)70. Samples, Gel bead-in-EMulsion (GEMs), and partitioning oil were loaded into Next GEM Chip K and placed in a Chromium Controller (10X Genomics) for single-cell encapsulation and recovery70. All protocol steps from GEM generation to library construction were completed using the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 5’ Reagent Kit v2 (Dual Index) and Library Construction Kit by 10X Genomics, according to the manufacturer’s instructions 70. cDNA was subjected to V(D)J amplification using Chromium Single Cell Human BCR Amplification Kit and Library Construction Kit by 10X Genomics, according to the manufacturer’s instructions70. Library quality was assessed based on fragment sizes and trace patterns using a High-Sensitivity DNA Analysis Kit and the Bioanalyzer 2100 instrument (Agilent Technologies, #NC1738319), as previously described70. Library quantification was performed using Quant-iT Picogreen dsDNA Assay Kit (Invitrogen, #P7589). Pooled libraries were sequenced on NovaSeq S4 flow cells at the Genomics Platform of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard70.

### Single-cell RNA/V(D)J data processing

CellRanger mkfastq (v5.0.1) was used to generate FASTQ files, as previously described70–72. Expression matrices were generated by CellRanger count (v6.0.1) with the genome reference (refdata-gex-GRCh38-2020-A), as previously described70–72. To remove ambient RNA, CellBender (v0.2.0) was run on matrices with the target false positive rate cutoff of 0.01, as previously described70,71. Poor quality cells were filtered out, as previously described70,71. Three doublet tools, Scrublet (v0.2.3), scDblFinder (v1.8.0), and scds (1.10.0) were used to calculate multiplet scores, as previously described70,71,73–75. CellRanger vdj (v6.0.1) was used with the flag of “--chain=IG” on FASTQ files with the VDJ reference file (refdata-cellranger-vdj-GRCh38-alts-ensembl-5.0.0)70–72.

### Single-cell V(D)J sequencing data processing and malignant plasma cell identification

Plasma cells were identified based on expression of key lineage markers and were considered for analysis (n=1,338,918), as previously described70,71. All V(D)J contigs detected by CellRanger (v6.0.1) were processed to identify a single heavy and light chain per cell barcode, as previously described70,71,76. Cells without V(D)J data (n=42,782) and with quality issues (n=3,657) (cells whose clonotype was highly similar but distinct from the main tumor) were excluded from analysis (n=46,439). The final number of plasma cells used for downstream analyses was 1,292,479. Clonotypic data from multiple samples, aliquots and timepoints were combined. Harmonized clonotypes were identified based on the frequency of unique CDR3 amino-acid (AA) sequences, as previously described76. Occasionally, clonotypes with only a heavy or light chain were identified; these single-chain clonotypes were collapsed with the matching two-chain clonotype with the highest frequency. By definition, CTCs shared the clonotype of BM tumor cells. Clones were sorted based on their cell count and candidate expanded clones were identified as clones with at least 20 cells at least twice the size of the next clone in order of frequency. Candidate expanded clones were then manually reviewed and considered malignant, if: (i) its immunoglobulin isotype matched that reported clinically through IFX, (ii) key MM oncogenes were expressed in accordance with tumor cytogenetics by FISH, and (iii) key immunophenotypic markers of plasma cell malignancy were up- or down-regulated. Secondary expanded clones (<50-100 cells) that clustered with normal plasma cells, had not been clinically detected as M-protein spikes in SPEP and IFX, and did not show high expression of key MM oncogenes or immunophenotypic markers were considered normal. In three patients, a clinically undetected second tumor was identified; in the absence of IFX or FISH, clones were considered malignant based on separate clustering from normal cells and expression of MM oncogenes and immunophenotypic markers, as previously described70,71. Gene-level clonotypes were derived by selecting the V(D)JC genes used most frequently within a particular clone. Tumor cells were detected in 72 of 73 patients, and in 3 patients, two tumors with distinct V(D)J re-arrangements were detected, for a total of 75 tumors. For downstream analyses, CTC burden was estimated as the proportion of malignant plasma cells out of malignant and normal plasma cells.

### Transcriptional correlation analysis

Tumors with at least 30 cells in both compartments (BM and CTCs) were considered for this analysis (n=51). Highly variable genes (n=1,369) were selected using Scanpy’s (v1.8.2) highly_variable_genes function. Their log1p-normalized expression was averaged across tumor cells within each tumor by compartment. Correlation coefficients were computed using two-sided Spearman’s method.

### DNA Library Construction

CD138+ BM underwent DNA isolation (Thermo Fisher, #KIT0103) and library preparation (New England Biolabs, #E6177) with unique dual index adapters, according to the manufacturer’s instructions, as previously described11. Final library fragment sizes were assessed using the BioAnalyzer 2100 (Agilent Technologies), with yields quantified by a Qubit 3.0 fluorometer (Thermo Fisher) and qPCR (Roche, #KK4824), as previously described11.

### Whole Genome Sequencing and Genomic Data Analysis

Final libraries were normalized and pooled and sequencing was performed on NovaSeq S4 flow cells at the Genomics Platform of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, as previously described11. WGS analysis was performed on an in-house cloud-based HPC system for copy-number and structural variant analyses, as previously described11. Sequencing reads were aligned to the hg19 reference genome with the bwa mem v0.7.7 algorithm, duplicate reads were marked with MarkDuplicates from Picard v1.457, indels were realigned with GATK 3.4 IndelRealigner, and base qualities were recalibrated with GATK 3.4 Base Recalibrator software, as previously described11. Small indels were called with with Strelka2 and were filtered (i) against a panel of normal, (ii) for potential technical artifacts (OxoG), and (iii) for multiple alignment with BLAT70,71,77. Structural variants were detected and filtered, as previously described70,71,78.

### Cell cycle scoring & determination of cell cycle phase

Cell cycle scores were obtained using S phase and G2M phase gene lists by Tirosh et al. and the score_genes_cell_cycle function in Scanpy (v1.8.2)79,80. To determine appropriate S and G2M score thresholds to assign cells into cell cycle phases, we first set the S score threshold at the 99.9th percentile of the respective distribution for normal plasma cells from healthy donors (n=180,790), which were assumed to show little proliferation (1 in 1000). We set the G2M score threshold at the 99.9th percentile of the respective distribution for normal plasma cells from healthy donors that did not pass the S phase threshold. Subsequently, we iteratively updated the S score threshold by setting it to the 99.9th percentile of S scores in non-G2M normal plasma cells until the updated threshold is <0.01 different from the prior threshold. This approach resulted in an S score threshold of ~0.1106 and a G2M score threshold of ~0.1060. Cells were assigned to the S phase if their S score was >~0.1106, and cells that were not assigned to the S phase were assigned to the G2M phase if their G2M score was >~0.1060, as previously described81,82.

### Differential expression and pathway enrichment analyses

Tumors with at least 30 cells in the BM and PB were selected for differential expression analysis (n=51). Differential expression analysis comparing CTCs and BM tumor cells within a particular patient (or tumor, for patients with multiple tumors) was conducted at the single-cell level using two-sided Wilcoxon’s rank-sum tests and the Benjamini-Hochberg approach to correct for multiple hypotheses testing, as implemented in the sc.tl.rank_genes_groups (Scanpy v1.8.2)80. Genes detected in less than 5% of tumor cells considered in this analysis were removed from consideration. Mitochondrial, immunoglobulin, and ribosomal genes were also removed from consideration. A total of 7,751 genes were considered for differential expression analysis. Genes that were significantly (adjusted p <0.05) upregulated (log fold-change >0) in >60% (n=30) of CTC-BM pairs were considered as hits (n=827) and were subjected to pathway enrichment analysis. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed using one-sided hypergeometric tests against the Hallmark pathway collection and p-values were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg approach, as previously described76,81,82.

### Circulatory capacity signature and scoring

A circulatory capacity signature was derived by sorting genes significantly upregulated in CTC samples compared to paired BM tumor cells by the number of CTC samples they were upregulated in as well as the average log fold-change in those samples and selecting the top 100 genes. Cells were scored for the circulatory capacity signature using Scanpy’s score_genes function (Scanpy v1.8.2) and were determined to be of high circulatory capacity if their score was higher than the 1st quartile of the circulatory score distribution in CTCs80. The proportion of BM tumor cells of high circulatory capacity was computed separately for each tumor and used for downstream analyses.

### Analyses of the CoMMpass dataset

Processed bulk RNA-seq data and metadata were downloaded from the MMRF Researcher Gateway (IA22 release). Patients baseline BM samples were scored for circulatory capacity by taking the mean expression of genes in the circulatory signature (n=99/100 were present in this dataset) and split into groups of high and low circulatory capacity based on the median distribution. The variable “D_IM_FLOWCYT_PCT_PC_IN_PB_HIGH” was used as an estimate of the patients’ CTC burden by flow cytometry and the variable “KEATSPROLIF_INDEX” was used as an estimate of the tumors’ proliferative capacity. The tumors’ cytogenetic status was derived from the dataset’s WGS-based SeqFISH results; the variable “SeqWGS_Cp_Hyperdiploid_Call” was used to determine the tumors’ hyperdiploidy status and variables “SeqWGS_Cp_1q21_20percent” and “SeqWGS_Cp_13q14_20percent” were used to determine the tumors’ Amp1q and Del13q status. Tumors with a primary Ig translocation were classified as such; tumors without a primary Ig translocation were classified as HRD (when present). Overall survival analysis was performed using the Kaplan-Meier method with a two-sided log-rank test or, for multivariate analysis, Cox proportional hazards regression as implemented in the R packages survival (v3.5.5) and survminer (v0.4.9), as previously described81,82.

### Copy number and phylogenetic analysis

Copy number variants (CNVs) were inferred using Numbat (v1.1.0), as previously described39,70,71. Allelic data was collected from malignant and normal plasma cells and B cells from both BM/PB to ensure the frequency of CNVs and particularly, clonal deletions, would not negatively impact genotyping and phasing in samples with high tumor purity, as previously described70,71,76,81,82. Furthermore, a custom panel of 1.2K healthy donor plasma cells was used to correct for cell type-specific expression patterns, such as immunoglobulin expression, which otherwise results in artifactual CNV inference on chromosomes 2, 14, and 22, as previously described70,71,76,81,82. Ultimately, CNVs were inferred on a combined list of tumor cell barcodes from baseline BM/PB samples for each tumor (n=75). Patients (n=17) were downsampled to 15K tumor cells prior to running Numbat. Numbat was run with max_iter=2, tau=0.1, min_cell=10.

A total of 58 tumors had CNVs detected, with 56 of them having at least 1 subclone, after filtering out clones with <50 cells. Clone-level probabilities were then computed as the median joint probability for each CNV across cells in the respective clone and CNVs were called if the median probability for the event in that clone was >0.65; if the event was deemed to be present in the clone immediately prior to the given clone, the event was called if the median probability in the given clone was >0.55. Variants not called in any clone were removed from consideration and clones with identical CNV profiles were collapsed together. Clone-level CNV profiles were then used for phylogenetic tree inference via maximum parsimony analysis, using the R package phanghorn (v2.11.1)83.

Numbat CNV calls were translated into focal, arm-level, or chromosome-level calls in the following manner: for each segment, its overlap with both the p and q arms of the corresponding chromosome was computed; if the overlap was >0.85, the event was called an arm-level event for that particular arm, otherwise it was called a focal event; if both arms of a particular chromosome were involved by a single event at the arm level, the event was called a chromosome-level event.

### Comparison of clone frequency in BM tumor cells and CTCs

Analysis was performed in 35 tumors which had both subclones and at least 100 CTCs. Clone frequency was compared between BM and PB across tumors and clones using a two-sided Pearson’s correlation approach. For patient-specific analyses, 2,000 tumor cells were randomly sampled per compartment (BM vs PB) and UMAP embeddings were generated off of the downsampled cell-level joint probabilities for CNVs that were called in the tumor’s clones using the uwot (v0.2.1) R Package with n_neighbors = 5084. Subclone frequencies and their 95% confidence intervals were computed out of the sampled 2,000 tumor cells for visualization purposes.

### Comparison of circulatory capacity between tumor subclones

Tumor cells from patients with subclonal Amp1q (n=12) or Del13q (n=20) were selected for downstream analysis. Within each tumor, the proportion of BM tumor cells with high circulatory capacity (> 1st quartile of the CTC distribution) was computed separately for subclones carrying Amp1q or Del13q and subclones without these events. These proportions were then compared across tumors for each abnormality using two-sided paired Wilcoxon tests.

### Cytogenetic classification & cell downsampling

All cells were scored for MM signatures reported by Zhan et al. using Scanpy’s (v1.8.2) score_genes function38,80. After normalizing each signature across cells, median scores were calculated within tumor cells per compartment and patient. Median signature scores and mean log1p-transformed gene expression values for MM oncogenes (CCND1, CCND2, NSD2, FGFR3, MAF, MAFB) within tumor cells per patient and compartment were used as features in a multivariate logistic regression model to detect IgH translocations. Features were selected based on established knowledge about their association with IgH translocations in MM38,60,61. BM tumor cells (n=50) with either an IgH translocation or hyperdiploidy (HRD) by FISH (n=38) or research-level WGS (n=36) were used to train the model iteratively following a leave-one-out approach. Since we infer the presence of a translocation and cannot determine whether it is IgH, IgK or IgL that is translocated next to the respective partner gene, we opted for using terminology that is focused on the affected partner gene (for example, “CCND1 Trx“ instead of t(11;14)). A sole tumor with t(8;14) (IgH-MAFA) translocation by WGS, was removed from the training cohort to avoid overfitting. HRD cases were used as controls for the model to detect the presence of one of four IgH translocation types: CCND1 Trx, NSD2 Trx, MAF Trx, and MAFB Trx. No cases with t(6;14) had been detected by FISH or WGS, thus, no such cases were in the training cohort. We aggregated coefficients from the 50 leave-one-out models by taking the median and generated an aggregate model, whereby the probability for each class is computed using the equation: p j = exp ⁡ b 0 , j + b 1 , j * x 1 + ⋯ + b i , j * x i 1 + exp ⁡ b 0 , j + b 1 , j * x 1 + ⋯ + b i , j * x i , where j corresponds to a particular class and i corresponds to a particular feature. Subsequently, the tumor was classified as the class with the maximum probability, if that probability was larger than 0.5; alternatively, it was classified as “No Trx”. Tumors classified as having no IgH translocation (“No Trx”) were classified as HRD when Numbat detected at least two extra chromosomal copies in any autosomes39. Tumors without an IgH translocation according to the classifier or HRD according to Numbat were classified as “Other” (n=7); some of these (n=3) had no CNVs detected, while others (n=4) had CNVs but did not meet the criteria for HRD (i.e., at least two extra chromosomal copies). The one case with t(8;14) by WGS, and two cases with high CCND3 expression levels, were manually classified as MAFA Trx and CCND3 Trx, respectively. Three cases with discordant CTC and BM results were identified and their status was determined following manual review.

To assess for deterioration of the classifier’s performance, we performed downsampling with a range of cell numbers (1-100) and 10 iterations for each cell number. Cells were scored and the model was fit to obtain predicted classes. The classifier’s consistency over decreasing sample sizes was assessed as the proportion of 10 iterations per sample size tested for which the predicted class matched that obtained when all available cells were used. The classifier’s accuracy per sample size tested was assessed as the proportion of samples for which the predicted class from CTCs matched that obtained by FISH at least 90% of the time (i.e., 9/10 iterations).

### Statistics and Reproducibility

For cohort design, we estimated the number of cases required to profile at least 5 patients with t(11;14), t(4;14), and t(14;16) or t(14;20), assuming binomially distributed successes with probabilities of 0.2, 0.15, and 0.1, respectively. We estimated that a cohort of 70 patients would result in a probability of >0.8 for all three major classes to be represented with a frequency of at least 5 patients/class. No data were excluded from the analyses, unless stated otherwise (for example, removing individuals without tumor cells or with rare cytogenetic profiles from cytogenetics-based comparisons). No randomized experiments were included, and data collection and analysis were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments. Statistical tests used are mentioned in main text or figure legends, and non-parametric tests were preferred. Additional research design information is available in the Reporting Summary.
